source_text: Capitula xxxiii (definitiones passionum animae rationalis) ΕΥΑΓΡΙΟΥ ΜΟΝΑΧΟΥ ΚΕΦΑΛΑΙΑ ΛΓʹ ΚΑΤ' ΑΚΟΛΟΥΘΙΑΝ. Αʹ. Ἴκτερος, ἔστιν ἕξις χειρίστη ψυχῆς λογικῆς, καθ' ἣν ἐσφαλμένως Θεόν τε καὶ τὴν τῶν γεγονότων θεωρίαν ὁρᾷ. 40.1265 Βʹ. Ὀπισθότονος, ἔστι κακία φύσεως λογικῆς, καθ' ἣν δυσκαμπὴς γίνεται πρὸς ἀρετὴν καὶ γνῶσιν τὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ. Γʹ. Σφακελλισμὸς, ἔστι ζέσις καὶ κίνησις θυμοῦ τὸ λογιστικὸν μέρος τῆς ψυχῆς ἐκταράττουσα. ∆ʹ. Τυφλότης, ἔστιν ἄγνοια τοῦ νοῦ, ταῖς πρακτικαῖς ἀρεταῖς καὶ τῇ τῶν γεγονότων θεωρίᾳ μὴ ἐπιβάλλουσα. Εʹ. Παράλυσις, ἔστι δυσκινησία λογιστικῆς ψυχῆς πρὸς τὰς πρακτικὰς ἀρετάς. ϛʹ. Γονόῤῥοια, ἔστι ῥᾳθυμία λογικῆς ψυχῆς, καθ' ἣν ἀποβάλλειν τοὺς τῆς πνευματικῆς διδασκαλίας εἴωθε λόγους. Ζʹ. Ἀποκάθισις, ἔστιν ἀδυναμία λογικῆς ψυχῆς, καθ' ἣν τὰς συντελούσας ἀρετὰς πρὸς τὴν μόρφωσιν τοῦ Χριστοῦ εἴωθεν ἀποβάλλειν. Ηʹ. Λέπρα ἀπιστία ἐστὶν λογικῆς ψυχῆς, καθ' ἣν οὐ πληροφορεῖται ψηλαφῶσα τοὺς λόγους.
thought_title: Eight diseases of the rational soul
orientation: Evagrius opens his list of thirty-three definitions by naming eight diseases of the rational soul, each defined as a disposition, vice, movement, or ignorance that hinders virtue and knowledge of God.
pass_a_gloss: Thirty-three chapters (definitions of the passions of the rational soul). Of Evagrius the monk, thirty-three chapters in sequence. 1. Jaundice is a worst disposition of the rational soul, according to which it sees wrongly both God and the contemplation of the things that have come to be. 2. Opisthotonos is a vice of the rational nature, according to which it becomes hard to bend toward virtue and the knowledge of God. 3. Sphakelismos is a boiling and a movement of anger that throws into confusion the reasoning part of the soul. 4. Blindness is an ignorance of the mind that does not apply itself to the practical virtues and to the contemplation of the things that have come to be. 5. Paralysis is a difficulty of movement of the reasoning soul toward the practical virtues. 6. Gonorrhea is a slackness of the rational soul, according to which it is accustomed to throw away the words of spiritual teaching. 7. Apokathisis is a weakness of the rational soul, according to which it is accustomed to throw away the virtues that contribute to the formation of Christ. 8. Leprosy is unbelief of the rational soul, according to which it is not fully assured when it touches the words.

choices.why: The brief mandates 'disposition' for ἕξις; χειρίστη is superlative of κακός, so 'worst' preserves the superlative force.
The brief's glossary requires 'rational soul' for ψυχὴ λογική, and the genitive here is the same phrase.

choices.english: the contemplation of the things that have come to be
choices.why: θεωρία is 'contemplation' per the brief; γεγονότων is the perfect participle of γίγνομαι, so 'the things that have come to be' renders the perfect aspect literally.
rejected: the theory of what has happened

choices.why: The brief mandates 'vice' for κακία; φύσεως λογικῆς is 'rational nature' (not 'rational soul' here, since φύσις is used, not ψυχή).

choices.english: a boiling and a movement of anger
choices.why: ζέσις is literally 'boiling' or 'seething'; θυμός is 'anger' or 'spirit' in its irascible sense; the two nouns are coordinated, so both get articles in English.
rejected: a seething and motion of wrath
a boiling and stirring of the temper

choices.why: The brief mandates 'ignorance' for ἄγνοια and 'mind' for νοῦς; the genitive is subjective, so 'of the mind'.

pass_b_english: Jaundice is the worst disposition of the rational soul, by which it sees God and the contemplation of the things that have come to be in a distorted way.
Opisthotonos is a vice of the rational nature, by which it becomes hard to bend toward virtue and the knowledge of God.
Sphakelismos is a boiling and a movement of anger that throws the reasoning part of the soul into confusion.
Blindness is ignorance of the mind that does not lay hold of the practical virtues and the contemplation of the things that have come to be.
Paralysis is a difficulty of movement in the rational soul toward the practical virtues.
Gonorrhea is a slackness of the rational soul, by which it habitually casts away the words of spiritual teaching.
Sitting-down is a weakness of the rational soul, by which it habitually casts away the virtues that contribute to the formation of Christ.
Leprosy is unbelief of the rational soul, by which, though handling the words, it is not fully assured.

problems.quote: A discharge is a weakness of the rational soul, by which it habitually casts away the virtues that contribute to the formation of Christ.
problems.source_quote: Ἀποκάθισις, ἔστιν ἀδυναμία λογικῆς ψυχῆς, καθ' ἣν τὰς συντελούσας ἀρετὰς πρὸς τὴν μόρφωσιν τοῦ Χριστοῦ εἴωθεν ἀποβάλλειν.
problems.fix: Reconstitution is a weakness of the rational soul, by which it habitually casts away the virtues that contribute to the formation of Christ.
problems.ruling: ἀποκαθίσις in medical context means discharge/excretion, but here as spiritual metaphor paired with γονόρροια, 'discharge' is contextually appropriate; not a major error.

problems.quote: Leprosy is unbelief of the rational soul, by which it does not gain full assurance when it touches the words.
problems.source_quote: Λέπρα ἀπιστία ἐστὶν λογικῆς ψυχῆς, καθ' ἣν οὐ πληροφορεῖται ψηλαφῶσα τοὺς λόγους.
problems.why: The Greek says the soul is not informed by the words; English adds “full assurance” and misstates the mechanism.
problems.fix: Leprosy is unbelief of the rational soul, by which it is not informed by the words.
problems.ruling: πληροφορεῖται means 'to be fully assured/ convinced'; 'gain full assurance' is correct. ψηλαφῶσα means 'touching/groping'; 'when it touches' is accurate. No major error.

edits.old: A discharge is a weakness of the rational soul, by which it habitually casts away the virtues that contribute to the formation of Christ.
edits.new: Reconstitution is a weakness of the rational soul, by which it habitually casts away the virtues that contribute to the formation of Christ.

fixed: Ἀποκάθισις means 'restitution' or 'recovery,' not 'discharge'; changed to 'Reconstitution.'
The Greek πληροφορεῖται means 'is informed,' not 'gains full assurance'; changed to 'is not informed by the words.'

problems.why: Ἀποκάθισις means 'sitting down/relapse,' not 'reconstitution'; medical term for reclining posture.
problems.fix: Sitting-down or Relapse is a weakness of the rational soul...
problems.ruling: Greek Ἀποκάθισις = ‘sitting down, relapse’, not ‘reconstitution’; translation changes meaning.

problems.quote: it is not informed by the words
problems.why: πληροφορεῖται means 'fully convinced/assured,' not 'informed'; ψηλαφῶσα means 'touching/groping.'
problems.fix: by which, though groping the words, it is not fully assured.
problems.ruling: οὐ πληροφορεῖται ψηλαφῶσα τοὺς λόγους = ‘is not understood, groping the words’; ‘not informed by the words’ omits groping and mis‑uses πληροφορεῖται.

fixed: The reasoning part of the soul: the source uses 'τὸ λογιστικὸν μέρος τῆς ψυχῆς' (the reasoning part of the soul) in chapter 3, while other chapters use 'ψυχὴ λογική' (rational soul). These are distinct terms in the source, so the English correctly reflects the variation.

The contemplation of the things that have come to be: the source consistently uses 'τὴν τῶν γεγονότων θεωρίαν' (the contemplation of the things that have come to be), which the English renders accurately.
Practical virtues: the source uses 'πρακτικαὶ ἀρεταί' (practical virtues), which the English renders accurately.
Gonorrhea: the source uses 'γονόρροια' (gonorrhea), which the English renders accurately. The medical term is the source's own metaphor.
Sitting-down: the source uses 'ἀποκάθισις' (sitting-down), which the English renders accurately.
The rational soul: the source uses 'ψυχὴ λογική' (rational soul) in most chapters, which the English renders accurately.
Groping the words: the source uses 'ψηλαφῶσα' (groping, handling, touching), and 'handling' better captures the sense of tactile examination, so I edited it.
